bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears.confidence_note: Two outside records were added in round 41 and checked. Neither carries this card's harm at this place with a link to the credit, so the card stays contested, better evidenced than before. First, Tanzania's Controller and Auditor General, in the annual audit of development projects for the year ended 30 June 2017 (AGR/DP/2016/2017) — the project's closing year — reports under significant finding (a) that people affected by three projects had not been paid compensation totalling TZS 11,870,767,751, and schedule 1(i) lists the Transport Sector Support Programme (TSSP) at TZS 36,826,419 unpaid; the same report's tables identify TSSP as World Bank funded with seven audits that year. The checker read the Swahili text of the finding, the schedule and the funder table. The audit gives no site and no number of people, and the word Bukoba appears nowhere in or near the finding, so the figure is a project-level fact covering the roads and all four airports. Attributing it to Bukoba rests on the completion report's own statement that no resettlement was needed elsewhere, which is the lender's account, so the site does not come from outside the lender. Second, the High Court of Tanzania at Bukoba decided Land Case No. 6B of 2010, Regina Peter Kamugisha vs Airport Manager Bukoba Airport & others, [2018] TZHC 2657, on 10 May 2018, eleven months after the credits closed. The judgment itself has not been read by anyone: TanzLII's document pages answer HTTP 403 behind a Cloudflare interstitial on every path tried, including /source, /source.pdf, the www host, the old /tz/judgment/ form and guessed media host filenames, so every detail here is TanzLII's search index, its own case note and highlighted page snippets, each of which the checker re-ran. The index carries: the suit was instituted on 11/10/2010 and the court sat on 9 and 10 May 2018; the plaintiff is "a widow and reside of Kashai, Municipality of Bukoba", aged 59, suing as administratrix of the estate of Peter Kamugisha; the defendants are the Airport Manager, Bukoba Airport, the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Infrastructure & Development and the Attorney General, with Kagera Co-operative Union (1990) Ltd as third party; the dispute follows the government's acquisition of her plot No. 142 Block "Z" at Kashai; the third party was paid a total of TZS 132,330,000 for land measured at 4,768 square metres; the entire compensation schedule, covering plots 109 to 145 in the Kashai area, was admitted as exhibit D2; she claimed a further TZS 10,000,000 for disturbance; she had complained in writing about the payment to the third party in 2009; and TanzLII's case note says a registered owner is entitled to compensation where the state paid a third party without proper title, with building value and general damages awarded. The case note does not say which defendant was held liable or what sum was awarded, and no document found ties this case to the five the completion report counted, which carry no case numbers. The acquisition and payment it concerns also sit outside the credit: the Tanzania Airports Authority's own resettlement plan update for Bukoba Airport, disclosed in 2016, records that compensation under the 2008 valuation report was finished "by the time the World Bank got involved in the phase II of the project in 2010". So the one site-exact outside record is probably about works this credit did not pay for. The completion report's other claims — the school move, the quarry families, Zanzibar — remain the lender's own.

field_changes.outcome: The credits closed on 20 June 2017, two years after the original closing date. Five resettlement cases at Bukoba were still unresolved at closure, four of them before the courts and one with payment outstanding. The Tanzania Airports Authority's own resettlement plan update for the airport, disclosed in 2016, gives the same five from the implementing side and breaks them down: three court cases, one project-affected person who could not be traced, and one who complained to the grievance committee, was not satisfied and intended to appeal to court; it also records 41 project-affected persons plus Tumaini Primary School at phase II, and that of 30 people entitled to interest for late payment of compensation, 25 had been paid and five had not. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the project team subsequently told it that the high court cases on carrying out the resettlement plan had been ruled on and that payment of compensation to the affected people was being processed; that statement is attributed to the project team and not to a document. The completion report of 16 January 2018 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed. Outside the lender, Tanzania's Controller and Auditor General reports for the project's closing year that TZS 36,826,419 of compensation was unpaid to people affected by this project, one of three projects whose unpaid compensation he totals at TZS 11,870,767,751; that figure is for the project as a whole and the audit does not say where or to how many people. Also outside the lender, the High Court of Tanzania at Bukoba decided Land Case No. 6B of 2010, Regina Peter Kamugisha vs Airport Manager Bukoba Airport & others, on 10 May 2018, a claim over the acquisition of plot No. 142 Block "Z" at Kashai in which, on TanzLII's case note, the court held a registered owner entitled to compensation where the state had paid a third party without title; no document ties that case to the five, and the payment it disputes was made before the Bank's credit. The Kamugisha facts are read off TanzLII's search index and snippets; the judgment itself cannot be opened.

corrections: The card treats the Bukoba resettlement cases as arising within the credit. The one Bukoba airport compensation case identifiable outside the lender was instituted on 11 October 2010, before the credits became effective on 1 December 2010, and an index snippet has the plaintiff complaining in writing about the payment to the third party in 2009, before Board approval on 27 May 2010. The Tanzania Airports Authority's own 2016 resettlement plan update puts that beyond snippets: it records that compensation of the people identified in the 2008 valuation report was already finished by the time the Bank became involved in phase II in 2010, that four plot owners from that valuation "were fully compensated then", and that the phase II valuation was commissioned only in 2012. So disputes over the earlier acquisition and payments were carried into the project's resettlement plan rather than created by it.

The card says the Bank's documents give no count of people. The Tanzania Airports Authority's 2016 resettlement plan update, disclosed through the Bank, does: 14 affected people under the 2008 valuation, 15 in the 2009 plan, 41 plus Tumaini Primary School by phase II, 33 interviewed in its socio-economic survey, 30 entitled to interest for late payment of whom 25 were paid, and the five pending payments broken down as three court cases, one person untraceable and one grievance complainant. It also records that a resettlement audit commissioned in 2015 at the Bank's direction found the 2009 plan's implementation did not fully comply with OP 4.12 or Tanzanian law.

The round 41 entry said the Kamugisha claim "succeeded against the airport manager, the ministry and the Attorney General". TanzLII's case note does not apportion liability among the defendants and gives no sum; it says only that a registered owner is entitled to compensation where the state paid a third party without title, with building value and general damages awarded. The claim that it succeeded against all three named defendants is not carried by anything readable.

bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears.what_it_does_not_settle: Where the TZS 36,826,419 was owed, or to how many people, so the Bukoba attribution is inference resting on the lender's own account of the other sites. Whether the Kamugisha case is one of the five the completion report counted; no document found says so and the Bank's documents give no case numbers. Whether this credit paid for the works her land was taken for: the Airports Authority's own plan update puts the 2008 valuation's compensation before the Bank's phase II involvement in 2010. What sum the court awarded or which defendant paid it. Nothing outside the lender records the five cases as five, the entitlement agreed through the grievance mechanism, the amount outstanding from the Tanzania Airports Authority, or the later statement that the cases had been decided and payment was being processed; and nothing outside the lender records the relocation of Tumaini Primary School, the more than 50 disabled children in its unit, the longer journeys to school, the quarry families on the Arusha to Minjingu road, or the cemetery moved at Zanzibar. And because TanzLII's documents will not open on any route, no sentence of the Kamugisha judgment has been read.

The snippets give the defendants as the National Irrigation Authority and the National Land Commission, the project as "Lower Nzoia Irrigation and Flood Mitigation", a witness as a senior irrigation engineer, and the project management unit's recommendation as either "compensation of all assets within the homestead" with resettlement, or realigning the canal to avoid the suit property. Who won is not known. The Land Acquisition Tribunal, which round 38 found is where Kenyan unpaid-compensation claims land, holds no Lower Nzoia case: the consolidated tribunal judgments against the National Irrigation Authority are about the Lower Kuja scheme in Migori. A third outside record, added at checking: the National Land Commission's own gazette notices for this scheme. Gazette Notice No. 15518, in the Kenya Gazette of 22 November 2024, sets out the compulsory acquisition of land for part of the Lower Nzoia Irrigation and Flood Mitigation project for the Ministry of Water, Sanitation and Irrigation and calls an inquiry to hear claims to compensation, on named dates and at named places in Busia County, six months before the credit closed; Notices 14030 and 14031 of 11 November 2022 cite a run of earlier notices from 2020, 2021 and 2022, and a further notice appears in the gazette of 1 August 2025, after closing. That is the Kenyan state's own record that land for this scheme was still being taken and compensation claims still being heard at and after the credit's closing date. It is read off Kenya Law's index and page snippets; the gazette pages answer HTTP 202 with an AWS WAF challenge and an empty body, so no gazette page has been opened and no notice's claimants, parcels or sums are known.

field_changes.outcome: The Bank's two documents on this project say different things about its resettlement performance, and both are given here. The completion report says the project complied with the resettlement policy OP 4.12 and that the social safeguards rating 'mostly remained Moderately Satisfactory' including at closing. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the same report says 'the rating for Involuntary Resettlement was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory (MU) by 2018 and remained MU until 2022 when it was upgraded to Moderately Satisfactory', with the other social safeguard policies staying moderately satisfactory. At closing 568 claimants worth about US$883,000 were still unpaid, and the Bank said it would monitor the post-closure safeguard action plan twice a year, including through the follow-on project. Of the irrigation works, supporting structures for a second phase were built, and the completion report records that land compensation and related social and environmental problems delayed handing sites to the contractor. Outside the lender, the Kenya News Agency reported on 31 October 2022 that the project might stall over the failure to complete compensation to the occupants of the land the canal crosses, with the National Irrigation Authority's officers blaming politics around land and the Siaya governor asking that people be paid for their land and property in time to save the project; and an affected landowner sued the Authority and the National Land Commission in the Environment and Land Court over the same scheme in 2022, a case decided on 24 January 2025, four months before the credit closed. The court facts are read off Kenya Law's search index and snippets; the judgment itself cannot be opened.

kenya-1991-university-fees-esac.confidence_note: This is a 1991 structural-adjustment case and the judgment indexes cannot hold it; recording their silence would be recording nothing. Kenya Law's earliest 1991 material is legal-notice metadata (for example Income Tax Act exemption notices published in Kenya Gazette Vol. XCIII), with no gazette text and no judgments of the period, and the National Assembly's online Hansard is the current session only, so neither Hansard nor the national archives, whose site did not serve, could be searched for the 1991 fee debate. Outside the lender, one contemporaneous official record was found and it corrects the card. The United States Department of State's Country Report on Human Rights Practices for 1991, published in February 1992, records that on 30 June, during a riot over student allowances, "one Moi University student, Shadrack Opiyo, was shot dead by the police". It adds that no investigation followed. That is the same date and the same single death as the event the Social Conflict Analysis Database codes, which the card describes as a nationwide protest against the raising of university fees; the identification is inferred from date and death count, not stated by either source. The grievance, on the outside record, is student allowances rather than fees, and the place is Moi University rather than nationwide or Nairobi; the card's point sits at Nairobi. The fee itself is corroborated outside the lender by a Kenyan academic record: Okuro, "Financing Higher Education in Kenya, 1960-2012", East African Journal of Education Studies 7(4), 2024, which dates a radical policy shift to 1991, attributes it partly to continued World Bank and IMF pressure to cut state funding of higher education, and says that in the 1991-92 academic year "the government for the first time introduced the cost-sharing or user charges scheme" requiring public university students to pay fees. That is a journal article, not a judgment, audit or newspaper, so it strengthens the card without moving it. The KSh 6,000 figure, the Board-presentation condition and the 1995 tranche terms remain the lender's own.

field_changes.suppression: The Social Conflict Analysis Database (University of Texas) records a nationwide student protest against the raising of university fees on 30 June-1 July 1991 and codes it as met with lethal force, with one death. Outside the lender and outside that dataset, the United States Department of State's Country Report on Human Rights Practices for 1991, published in February 1992, records that on 30 June, during a riot over student allowances, "one Moi University student, Shadrack Opiyo, was shot dead by the police", and that no investigation followed the incident. The two records share a date and a single death, so they are probably the same event, but neither says so, and the State Department gives the grievance as student allowances and the place as Moi University, not fees and not Nairobi.
field_changes.killed_note: Not counted. The Social Conflict Analysis Database codes one death in the protest of 30 June-1 July 1991. The United States Department of State's Country Report on Human Rights Practices for 1991 names that death: Shadrack Opiyo, a Moi University student, shot dead by the police on 30 June 1991 during a riot over student allowances, with no investigation following. The death is therefore no longer unconfirmed, and it was caused by the police. It is still not counted here because the outside record gives the grievance as student allowances rather than the fee the credit required, and no document ties the shooting to the credit's conditions.

corrections: The card's suppression field says "No news report of this protest was found to confirm it." A contemporaneous official record does confirm a death on that date and names the person: the US State Department's human rights report for 1991 gives Shadrack Opiyo, a Moi University student, shot dead by police on 30 June 1991, with no investigation following.

The card describes the event as a protest against the raising of university fees. The outside record gives the grievance as student allowances, and the place as Moi University in Eldoret rather than the nationwide protest the dataset codes or the Nairobi point the card uses. The Bank's own credit touched both, since it introduced the KSh 6,000 charge and capped student loans at KSh 21,500, but the two sources do not describe the same grievance and the card should not present the death as a death over fees.
kenya-1991-university-fees-esac.what_the_outside_source_settles: That a student was shot dead by Kenyan police on 30 June 1991 in a university riot, who he was, where he studied, and that no investigation followed; and, from a Kenyan academic source, that direct fees at public universities began in the 1991-92 academic year under World Bank and IMF pressure to cut state funding of higher education.
kenya-1991-university-fees-esac.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether the dataset's event and the State Department's shooting are the same event, which rests on the shared date and the single death. Whether the riot was over the new fee, the capped loan, the cut allowance or all three. Everything specific to the credit: the KSh 6,000 charge as a condition of Board presentation, the third-tranche terms of up to KSh 50,000 and a minimum KSh 8,000, the arrears from 1992/93 and the "negligible" rating on loan reform are all from the Bank's own implementation completion report, which no outside document checks.
